Every session this semester has the same shape, so you always know what is coming. Each session lasts three hours and is split into eleven segments.

No stretch of talking from me runs longer than twenty five minutes. After each short explanation you do something yourself, such as answering a question, working through a small example or solving a problem on paper. Roughly half of every session is you doing and half is me explaining.

The words, and how they nest||0.all:
Three of these ideas nest inside one another: artificial intelligence, then machine learning, then deep learning. Data science sits outside that nesting. Artificial intelligence is the biggest circle. Machine learning is an approach inside artificial intelligence. Deep learning is a family of machine learning methods, and it uses large networks of simple calculations called neural networks. So each one is contained by the one before it.

Data science is the odd one out. It overlaps all of them and is contained by none of them. Data science is the craft of getting an answer out of data at all. That includes finding the data, cleaning it, questioning it and presenting it.

Much of that work involves no model whatever. A person who counts missing readings, checks units, and explains a trend is doing data science, even if no predictive model is ever built.

Artificial intelligence||0.all:
Artificial intelligence means any machine doing something that we would call intelligent. It names a goal. Many different techniques aim at that goal.

For example, a chess engine is artificial intelligence. So is a spam filter, which sorts unwanted email. A thermostat is not, because it follows one fixed rule and has no notion of doing better.

This is easy to confuse with machine learning. Machine learning is one particular way of achieving artificial intelligence. All machine learning is artificial intelligence. Most artificial intelligence in history was never machine learning, because it ran on rules that people wrote by hand.

So the phrase artificial intelligence tells you what someone wants to achieve. It does not tell you how they do it, and it does not mean that the system understands the problem the way a person does.

Two ways to make a computer decide||0.all:
This is the fourth segment, and it takes twenty five minutes. It is about two ways to make a computer decide something. Both ways take some inputs and produce an output. What differs is how the connection between the two is found.

In the first way, a person writes the rule. In the second way, the computer learns the rule from examples of inputs and the answers that went with them. Learning patterns from data and using them to make predictions is the second way.

Neither way is always better. If an established equation exists and its assumptions apply, the equation can be the better choice. We will work out together when each way fits.

Keep that question in mind. Think about what you would need. You would need the outcome, which is the failure. You would need the information that existed before the failure. And you would need to know how far ahead a warning would still be useful.

In twenty minutes you will answer a version of this question yourself. You will do it on paper, with a small table of numbers, with no computer and no formula.

Traditional programming, and machine lea.all:
This slide shows the actual idea of the course. It compares two ways of working.

The first is traditional programming. You work out the rule yourself and write it down. The computer takes your rule and some inputs, and it produces answers. If you know that power equals voltage times current, you can write that rule yourself.

The second is machine learning. Here you do not know the rule. What you have are examples. Each example has the inputs and the answer that followed. You give both to the computer, and the computer works out a rule from them.

After that, the rule it found can be used on new inputs, and it predicts the answers. So the roles are reversed. In traditional programming you supply the rule. In machine learning the computer supplies the rule, and you supply the examples.

When to write the rule, and when to lear.all:
How do you choose between the two ways? This slide gives you the criteria.

Write the rule yourself when a code of practice, a datasheet or a validated equation already gives you the answer. Write it yourself when the relationship is simple and well understood. Write it yourself when you must explain every decision, line by line, to a client or a regulator. And write it yourself when you have little or no historical data.

Let the computer infer the rule when nobody knows the rule, or it involves many variables acting on each other. Choose this when you have a reasonable number of past examples where you know both the inputs and the outcome. An early estimate can help with planning, if its error is small enough for the decision. Finally, you must be able to test the inferred rule on cases it has never seen.

An equation still needs correct units and valid assumptions, so the check is always yours.

Twelve cases show their inputs and their measured outcomes. Case thirteen shows only its inputs. Predict the outcome of case thirteen, and write one sentence explaining your choice.

Reading the pattern from twelve cases||0.all:
Let us read a pattern from the twelve cases. One approach is to compare cases that have similar inputs. Follow the five steps on the slide.

Step one. Look down the columns and ask which column seems to move together with the outcome. Ignore the others for now.

Step two. Find the two cases whose value in that column sits on either side of case thirteen's value. Step three. Look at their outcomes. The answer for case thirteen is probably between them. Estimating between two known points like this is called interpolation, and it is a good guess, though it is never a guarantee.

Step four. Adjust for anything else you noticed, such as a second column that also seems to matter. Step five. Write the number down, write why, and ask how confident you are and what would change your mind.

You have used a pattern in known examples to predict an unknown value. Comparing the prediction with the measured value tells you the size of the error.

The distance between your prediction and the star is the prediction error. It is the difference between what you predicted and what was measured. Keep the unit with it, because an error of three is meaningless until we know three of what. If we subtract in the same order each time. In this course we take the measured value minus the predicted value, a positive and a negative error will tell us whether we predicted too high or too low.

The dashed line shows one possible pattern in the data. A line is only one kind of pattern, and other shapes are possible.

One case cannot tell us how reliable a method is. With a single test we only see how it did this once. Later we will use many cases that were held back, and then the error means much more.

Two kinds of question||0.all:
This is the sixth segment, and it lasts fifteen minutes. We look at two kinds of question. One is predicting a number, and the other is predicting a category. Almost everything in this course is one or the other.

The kind of answer decides the task. If the answer is an amount, such as a torque or a number of days, the task is regression. If the answer is a choice from a list of labels, such as failure or no failure, the task is classification.

Categories can be stored as numeric codes, like zero and one. The digits alone do not decide the task. What matters is what the answer means.

Regression and classification||0.all:
The slide shows the two shapes. In regression, the answer is a number on a continuous scale. A continuous scale means the value can be any amount between two points, such as any torque between ten and sixty newton metres. To handle this we fit a line or curve through the cases, and we read the prediction from it.

In classification, the answer is one of a small set of labels. To handle this we look for a boundary that separates the labels, so that cases on one side get one label and cases on the other side get the other.

The same data can often support both. Four limits, and none of them go away||0.all:
These are four limits of machine learning, and none of them goes away with a better computer.

First, there may be no data, or too few observations. A model can only learn from what has been recorded. Second, the inputs may carry no useful signal. They may be weak or irrelevant to the outcome. Third, a better method may already exist. A known physical equation can beat a model. Fourth, the future may change. Conditions today can differ from the conditions in the past data.

A model can produce a prediction even when the data are unsuitable. It will not warn you. So for every problem, check whether the inputs and the testing support the use you intend.

These four are questions to investigate for each plant and each data set. Each one is a question to investigate in each case.

Every word we used today (1 of 3)||0.all:
This is the first of three glossary slides. It lists the words we used today with short definitions.

Artificial intelligence is any machine doing something we would call intelligent. It is a goal that many techniques aim at. Machine learning is inferring a rule from examples instead of writing it yourself. Deep learning is machine learning that uses large neural networks, and it belongs to Semester 2. Data science is the craft of getting a trustworthy answer out of data.

A dataset is a collection of data. In this lesson we use tables of observations. An example, also called a row or an observation, is one recorded case. In supervised learning, an example includes its observed target.

A feature is a column known before the outcome. It is an input to the prediction. The target, also called the label, is the column you are trying to predict.

Every word we used today (2 of 3)||0.all:
This is the second glossary slide.

Regression means predicting a number on a continuous scale. Classification means predicting which of a small set of categories a case belongs to. Binary classification has exactly two categories, such as pass or fail. Multi-class classification has three or more categories.

A prediction is the model's answer for a case. The error is the difference between the predicted value and the measured value.

Unseen data means cases that were not used to fit the model. To be useful, they must also be relevant to the intended use and free from leakage. If you test a model on cases that look nothing like real use, a good score tells you very little.

Every word we used today (3 of 3)||0.all:
This is the last glossary slide, with three terms.

Data leakage means accidentally giving the model information that it would not have in real use. Usually that is something only known after the outcome. The repair column from earlier is an example. We return to this in Week 10.

Generalisation asks whether a rule learned from past cases still works on new ones. That is what we really care about.

Association versus cause is the third. A model learns which columns move together. It knows nothing about the mechanism behind them. To show that one thing causes another, you need extra assumptions or a carefully designed study.

Eight questions to ask about any data pr.all:
This slide is a cheat sheet with eight questions to ask about any data problem. Keep this slide. You can use it for every project in this course.

One, what exactly am I predicting? Name the target column and its unit. Two, is it a number or a category? Numeric class codes are still categories. Three, what do I know beforehand? List the features and check each one. Would I really have it before the outcome?

Four, where does the data come from? Who measured it, how often, over what period, and is it kept anywhere? Five, would a rule or an equation do this better? If a code of practice or a validated formula answers it, use that.

Six, how will I know if I am wrong? You need cases the model has never seen, so decide now how you will hold some back. Seven, what does being wrong cost? A false alarm and a missed failure are not equally bad, and that decides which model you pick. Eight, do today's conditions still resemble the data? If the process, material or plant has changed, the model may be quietly obsolete.

In this class we work in the notebook, using Colab. The script is there for comparison if you are curious. It is optional, and it is not an extra upload.

Words we will use||1.all:
Four more words will appear all day. Python is the language. Code is the set of instructions written in that language. Running means asking the computer to carry out those instructions.

A cell is one block of a notebook. A code cell holds instructions that can run. A text cell holds an explanation written for a human reader, and it runs no instructions.

Output is the result that appears just below a code cell after it runs. Suppose a code cell asks the computer to add two and two. Underneath we will see four. That four is the output.

A notebook has two kinds of cell||0.all:
Every notebook is built from cells, and cells come in two kinds.

A code cell holds Python instructions. It has a small run button beside it. When we press the button, the computer reads the instructions and carries them out.

A text cell holds an explanation. We use it to tell the reader what the code is for, why we chose a certain approach, or what the result means. A text cell does not run Python, so pressing run on it only displays the formatted text.

The output always appears directly below the code cell that produced it. This keeps each result next to its cause.

Cells share one Python session||0.all:
All the code cells in a notebook share one Python session. A session is one running period of the computer working on our notebook. Think of it as a single shared whiteboard. Whatever one cell writes on the board, every other cell can read afterwards.

This matters because cells depend on each other. If the first cell stores a number, the second cell can use that number without writing it again.

It also means that the order in which we run cells decides what is on the board at any moment. We will see this with a small example. Remember the short rule on the slide. A code cell runs instructions, and a text cell explains them.

Before we write code, let us be clear about numbers. A number says how much or how many. Three items is a count, and two point five metres is a length. Whole numbers are used for counting. Decimal numbers, with a point in them, can describe part of a unit. Two point five metres is two whole metres and half a metre more.

A value is one piece of information, and the number two point five is a value. A measurement also needs a unit, such as metres. Python stores the number only. It does not attach the unit for us, so we must remember the unit ourselves, and a good habit is to write it in a name or a comment.

Give a value a name||0.all:
Computers become useful when we can give a value a name and reuse it. A name that refers to a value is called a variable.

Look at the line readings equals twelve. Here readings is the name, and twelve is the number it refers to.

The act of attaching a name to a value is called assignment. In Python the equals sign is read as assign. In Python the equals sign stores a value in a name. Python works out the right side first, then gives the result to the name on the left.

If we assign again later, the new value replaces the old one. The name keeps only the latest value.

The hash symbol starts a comment. A comment is a note for the person reading the code. The computer ignores everything after the hash on that line, so we can write explanations freely.

Think of a name tag. We first stick the tag thickness on one value. Later we run a new assignment that gives thickness a different value. The tag moves to the new value. Python does not keep a history of the old one under that name.

After the reassignment on this slide, thickness refers to zero point two zero. If we print thickness now, we see zero point two zero.

This is why the order of the lines in a cell matters. Python reads from the top down, and each assignment replaces the earlier one. When a result surprises us, a good first check is to ask which assignment ran most recently for that name.

Every value in Python has a type. The type is the kind of information, and it decides which operations are allowed.

The table lists five. An int is a whole number, like three. A float is a decimal number, like three point five. A str is text in quotes, such as the characters three, point, five inside quotation marks. A bool is True or False. And None is a special value that means no value was supplied.

The example shows why this matters. Three point five plus two is a number sum, and it gives five point five. But if both are in quotes, they are text, and plus now joins the text. The text three point five joined with the text two gives three point five two.

So quotes change the type, and the type changes what plus does. When a result looks odd, check the type first.

Operator||0.all:
An operator is a symbol that tells Python which operation to carry out.

You already know most of them. Plus adds. Minus subtracts. The star, which we write with the asterisk key, multiplies. The forward slash divides. Two stars in a row raise to a power, so two star star three means two to the power three.

There is one more, written as two slashes together. It divides and then rounds the answer down to a whole number. The word for that is floor division. As an example, minus five floor divided by two gives minus three, because the exact answer is minus two point five and rounding down takes us to minus three.

Why this week’s tools are needed||0.all:
Think about a sensor that measures something every minute and writes the results to a file. That file is a CSV file. Each line is one record, and the values on a line are separated by commas.

A real file can hold hundreds or thousands of records. We cannot type each one into our program by hand. We need a way to read them in, visit each one, and add them up.

So first we learn the Python tools for that job. Lists hold the readings. Loops visit them one by one. Dictionaries label the fields of a record. With those in place, we can read a whole file and summarise it in a few lines.

List and index||0.all:
A list holds several values in order. We write it with square brackets and commas between the values. Our example is the list two, four, six, and we give it the name readings.

Every item in a list has a position, and Python calls this position the index. The first item sits at position zero, the second at position one, and the third at position two. We count from zero.

To pick one item, we write the list name followed by square brackets with the position inside. So readings, open square bracket, zero, close square bracket, selects the first item, which is two.

Notice that square brackets appear in two jobs. Around values they build a list. After a name they select an item.

Position zero holds the value two. This is the first item in the list. Many people expect the first position to be one, so it takes practice to count from zero.

Position one holds four, and position two holds six.

This list has three items, so there is no position three. If we ask for position three, Python stops with an error message. The last position is always one less than the number of items. In this list the last position is two.

Keep this picture of positions zero, one and two in mind, because every list in this course works the same way.

A loop repeats instructions||0.all:
A loop runs a block of instructions more than once. One run through the block is called an iteration.

Python gives us two kinds of loop. The first is the for loop. It takes one item at a time from a collection, such as a list, and runs the same action on each item. We use it when every item needs the same treatment.

The second is the while loop. It keeps repeating as long as a condition stays true. A condition is a true or false question. We use while when a condition decides how long the repetition lasts.

Today we begin with for, because summing a list of readings is a job where every item gets the same treatment.

Reading is a name for the current item. Python gives this name the next item automatically each time round. We choose the name ourselves. Readings with an s is the list we are visiting. These are two different names. One is a single item and the other is the whole collection.

The word in links the item name to the collection.

The colon begins the loop body. The body is the set of lines that repeat, and we mark them with four spaces at the start of each line.

After the last item has been visited, Python leaves the loop and carries on below it.

Updating a counter inside a loop||0.all:
A counter records how many times something happens. We build one in two steps.

First, before the loop, we write count equals zero. This gives the counter a starting value.

Second, inside the loop, we write count equals count plus one. Python reads the right side first, takes the current count and adds one, and then stores the answer back in count.

There is a shorter way to write the same update. Count plus equals one means the same as count equals count plus one. In the same way, total plus equals reading means total equals total plus reading.

The starting value must be set outside the loop. If we reset count to zero inside the loop, it goes back to zero on every pass, and we lose the earlier count.

Accumulator||0.all:
An accumulator is a running total. It is a variable that collects a result a little at a time as a loop visits each item.

We build it in three steps. Before the loop, we set it to zero. Inside the loop, we add the current item to it. After the loop finishes, we read the final total.

Think of a cashier adding up a customer's items. The till starts at zero, each item adds to the total, and the last number on the screen is the answer.

The counter we saw a moment ago is an accumulator too. It adds one each time instead of adding the item's value.

A while loop checks before each repetiti.all:
A while loop checks a condition before each repetition. The condition here is count is less than three.

In the first step, Python tests the condition before entering the block. If the answer is true, it enters the block. If the answer is false, it skips the block and continues after the loop.

In the second step, at the end of the body, Python returns to the condition and tests it again. A for loop moves to the next item in a list by itself. A while loop does not do that. It only repeats the test.

The third step is about stopping. Something inside the loop must make the condition become false, or the loop may continue forever. In our example, count goes up by one on every iteration, so it eventually reaches three.

The last line has no indentation, so it runs once, after the loop ends.

The order is to set up, test, run the body, update, and test again. When count reaches three, the test is false and the loop stops. The output is zero, one, two, finished.

Choosing if for or while||0.all:
We now have three ways to control a program, and this table compares them.

An if statement chooses a path once. When the chosen block is done, the program moves on.

A for loop visits supplied items, such as the items of a list. It finishes when the items run out.

A while loop repeats as long as its condition is true. It finishes when the condition becomes false.

The key difference is between if and while. Both test a condition, but if tests it a single time. A while loop tests it again after each run of its body. So a condition alone does not mean a program repeats.

In the first step, range of three supplies zero, one and two. The stop value, three, is left out. Range of one, comma, four supplies one, two and three, because it starts at one and stops before four.

In the second step, we use range with a for loop. The loop still works the same way. It takes the next supplied number each time.

In the third step, a third value is the step. Range of zero, six, two supplies zero, two and four. The step is the amount we move between one number and the next. The step can never be zero.

The first is continue. It skips the rest of the current iteration and starts the next one. The loop carries on with the next item.

The second is break. It exits the loop immediately. Python resumes with the line after the loop. If there are loops inside loops, break exits only the nearest one.

The third point is about layout. The if condition sits inside the loop with four spaces. Its action, continue or break, sits inside the condition with eight spaces. That is an indented block inside another block. Each level of indentation tells Python what belongs to what.

A dictionary is a record with named fiel.all:
A dictionary is a record with named fields. In a list we find items by position. In a dictionary we find them by name.

Our example is record equals braces, with the word unit, a colon, and the letter A, then a comma, then the word reading, a colon and four. This stores two key and value pairs. The keys are the names of the fields, and the values hold the information.

The braces enclose the dictionary. A colon separates each key from its value, and a comma separates one pair from the next. Each key can appear only once.

To read a value, we write record, then square brackets with the key in quotation marks. Record with the key reading gives four. We ask for the field by its name, so we do not need to remember a position.

A missing dictionary key and get||0.all:
Sometimes we ask a dictionary for a key that is not there. Take a record that holds a unit and a reading. When we write record, then square brackets with the word reading in quotes, Python looks for the key called reading and gives back its value. If that key does not exist, Python stops with an error called KeyError.

There is a gentler way to ask. Record dot get, with the word missing in quotes and then zero, asks for the key called missing and says, if it is absent, give me zero instead. This call does not add a new key to the dictionary. It only hands back the fallback.

The second input to get is the fallback value. We use a fallback only when the task tells us what missing information should mean. In a count, for example, a missing key can sensibly mean zero so far.

The output is 4, then 6, then 0.

Tuples and unpacking||0.all:
A tuple stores items in order, like a list, but its positions cannot be reassigned. We write one with round brackets. Point equals open bracket 2, comma, 3, close bracket stores two coordinates. Point with zero in square brackets is 2, because counting starts at zero. If we try to put a new value into point at position zero, Python refuses.

Unpacking means giving the items of a tuple to separate names in one line. X comma y equals point gives the first item to x and the second to y. The number of names must match the number of items, otherwise Python reports an error.

A tuple stops us replacing its positions. If a tuple holds a list inside it, the items of that list can still change, because the tuple only fixes which object sits at each position.

The first print shows x, which is 2. The second print shows y, which is 3.

The original tuple still exists after unpacking. We have only copied its items into two names so that we can use them separately.

The output is 2, then 3.

A set remembers distinct items||0.all:
A set is a collection that keeps one copy of each distinct item. It is useful when the question is, have we seen this ID before? A sensor ID might appear fifty times in a file, and the set keeps it once.

To make an empty set we write seen equals set with empty brackets. Seen dot add with the letter A in quotes puts A into the set. To ask whether something is inside, we write the item, then the word in, then the set. Python answers True or False.

A set is the wrong tool when position or repeated readings matter, because a set has no positions and we cannot index it. One trap to remember is that empty curly brackets create an empty dictionary. For an empty set we always write set with brackets.

We start with an empty set called seen. Then we add the letter A. We add the letter A a second time. A set keeps only one copy of each item, so the second add changes nothing.

The first print shows len of seen, which counts the items. The answer is 1, because only one distinct ID is stored.

The second print asks whether A is in seen. The word in gives back True or False, and here it is True.

The third print asks about B. We never added B, so the answer is False.

The output is 1, True, False. This is how a set answers membership questions.

How the four collections differ||0.all:
We now have four collections, and each answers a different kind of question. We choose by the question we are asking.

If we have ordered readings, we use a list. We find items by position and the list can change.

If we have named fields, such as a unit and a reading belonging to one record, we use a dictionary. We find items by their key.

If we have fixed positions, such as a pair of coordinates, we use a tuple. Its positions cannot be reassigned.

If we only need to know which IDs we have already seen, we use a set. It keeps each distinct item once and answers yes or no.

Before writing code, we say the question aloud and pick the collection that fits it.

Here are two ways to reach the same number, 4. One uses a position and one uses a key, and they find it differently.

A list keeps items in order and numbers them starting at zero. When we ask for a position, Python counts along the list and returns whatever sits there. We need to know where the item is.

CSV and header||0.all:
CSV stands for comma-separated values. It is a plain text file where each line is usually one record, and the commas separate the fields on that line.

The first line is the header. It gives a name to each column, for example unit and reading. Every line after the header is data.

There is one important detail. Everything we read from a CSV file arrives as text, even a cell that looks like a number. The text two point five is not yet a number we can add. We have to convert it with float.

So when we read a CSV, we remember two things. The header gives us names for the columns, and every cell starts out as text.

When a group appears for the first time, it has no entry yet. We start it at zero before adding its first reading. The get function helps us do this in one step.

This slide shows where we are heading today. We will do two things.

First, we read a labelled table and select rows. A labelled table is a table where every column has a name at the top, like a sheet in Excel. Selecting rows means picking out only the records we want.

Second, we calculate column summaries and grouped totals. A column summary is one number that describes a whole column, such as an average. A grouped total is a total worked out separately for each group, such as the total energy for each building.

Last time we read a CSV file with the csv module and received lists of values. A DataFrame holds the same information, and it also remembers the column names for us.

What a filled value can and cannot tell.all:
Filling a missing value is useful, but we must understand what it means.

When we replace a blank with the median, the new number is an estimate. It is a sensible guess made by a rule. In our practice file, reading two had no ambient value, and we put in thirty. We do not know that the true temperature was thirty.

Because the filled number is a guess, it can change our averages and patterns. So we keep the original data, and we state the rule we used. That way, anyone can tell which values were recorded and which were estimated.

One more point. Our practice data is synthetic, which means it was made up for teaching. A pattern in it does not tell us how real equipment performs. We use it to practise the method.

An identifier is a label. The columns reading and record underscore id give each row a name so we can tell rows apart.

A label is only a name. The number on a reading does not tell us when it was taken. Reading four does not mean hour four, and reading two does not mean it was taken before reading three in real time. The numbers may have been assigned when the data was collected or when it was imported.

If we want to study a trend over time, we need a real timestamp, or a time sequence that has been written down and documented.

The same care applies to averages. An equipment mean describes the readings we have. In our practice data, M2 has a higher mean than M1. That does not prove M2 is faulty. Before anyone makes a decision about real equipment, we would look at representative measured data. For this teaching dataset, we only practise reading the numbers correctly.
